To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we generated an iPSc based BBB model of thyroid hormone transporter deficiency that showed that the blood-brain barrier was a major barrier to thyroid hormone entry into the brain and that a candidate drug could not enter the brain across the diseased BBB.

we used patient specific iPSCs to generate neural cells that showed a normal TH dependent neuronal phenotype, but that we identified a defect in the blood-brain barrier that could be a key contributor to the disease phenotype.

(1) MCT8 deficiency in iPSC-derived neural cells does not affect the ability of TH to regulate neural differentiation, maturation, and function; (2) MCT8 is necessary for the transport of active TH into the brain; and (3) a drug that crosses the normal BBB poorly does not cross a diseased BBB.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying human neurological diseases.
the study of human diseases using patient-specific induced pluripotent (iPSC) stem cells.
the development of novel therapeutic approaches to treat patients with severe mental retardation caused by a genetic defect in the thyroid hormone transporter MCT8.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BBB is the main site of action for MCT8 deficiency in vivo.
our results indicate that MCT8 is necessary to maintain the BBB integrity, and that the BBB is the main target of MCT8 mutations.
MCT8 is not required for TH dependent neural maturation and function, but that MCT8 deficiency causes a diseased BBB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MCT8 deficiency does not affect neural cells directly, but that it does cause a severe defect in the BBB that prevents active TH from reaching the brain.
the MCT8 deficiency is caused by a failure of the BBB to transport active TH into the brain, rather than an intrinsic defect in neural cells.

MCT8 deficiency causes a disease that is primarily mediated by a defective blood brain barrier (not by the neurons themselves), and this barrier defect can be circumvented by drug delivery to the brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that

MCT8 deficiency in neural cells does not cause the psychomotor retardations seen in MCT8 deficient patients, but instead the diseased phenotype arises from reduced entry of TH into the brain across the blood brain barrier.
the diseased BBB is a major factor underlying the pathophysiology of MCT8 deficient disease, and that circumventing the BBB could be a viable treatment strategy.
MCT8 deficiency is a disease of the BBB and not a disease of neurons.
